content: When evaluating arguments involving negation, focus on translating informal statements into their logical form to reveal how negation interacts with quantifiers and predicates. This process helps uncover hidden assumptions by clarifying whether a negation applies to an entire claim or just part of it—such as distinguishing between "not all" (which allows exceptions) and "none" (which is universal). Instead of following rigid steps, explore the logical relationships by asking: "If the premises are true, what must follow about the conclusion, especially when negation might shift the scope from universal to existential or vice versa?" Look for potential mismatches where a negated premise could introduce ambiguity, allowing cases where the premises hold but the conclusion fails. By emphasizing this exploration of relationships, you can naturally identify whether the argument is deductively valid or rests on a formal fallacy.
